newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech ultra-right party says police detain leader.
newsitem.headline: Czech ultra-right party says police detain leader.

text.p: Czech police detained ultra-right Republican party head Miroslav Sladek on Friday, a day after he lost his parliamentary immunity in a row over anti-German comments he is accused of making.

Jiri Zajic, secretary of the Republican parliamentary faction in the lower house, told Reuters Sladek was detained by police in front of the parliament building in central Prague as he arrived for the afternoon session.
"He was taken without any summons or without any official documents," Zajic said.
The Czech news agency CTK quoted the chairman of the lower house, Milos Zeman, as telling members of parliament that Sladek had been detained.
National police spokeswoman Ivana Moosova told Reuters that Sladek had been "summoned for an explanation" by police and he was not officially charged with a crime.
She said no warrant was needed under Czech law for such questioning.

The house agreed on Thursday to lift Sladek's parliamentary immunity and allow police to investigate anti-German remarks he is alleged to have made during a visit to Prague in January by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

Sladek has been quoted in local media as telling his followers during a demonstration that "we can only regret that we only killed a few Germans during the war". The remarks have been widely quoted, and never denied.

The Republican party has vehemently opposed a post-World War Two reconciliation agreement with Germany, signed by Kohl and Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus during the German chancellor's visit in January.

The Republicans, who won eight percent of the popular vote in last year's lower house elections, see the declaration as a betrayal of Czech interests, and tried in vain to block its approval by parliament earlier this month.

Two other Republican deputies, Josef Krejza and Rudolf Smucr, were also stripped of their immunity on Thursday. They may face charges for disrupting a Czech-German memorial meeting in the former Nazi concentration camp at Terezin in 1994.
